s-fa1-high-0.essay:
Most goodbye poems pick a side: the child either mourns home or celebrates getting out of it. Marisol Teague's "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" refuses to choose. Through the circular imagery of the laundromat, a line break that splits the mother's care in two, and a closing gesture that copies the very habits the speaker is leaving, Teague presents leaving as a form of thanks that cannot fully sound like thanks, because the mother's labor both made the departure possible and stands for the life the speaker wants to escape.

The poem begins by linking the two women through surrender. When the change machine takes the speaker's money, "I let it, the way she let the landlord" keep the deposit (line 3). The simile makes inheritance feel less like a gift than a habit of absorbing loss. Even before the hands appear, the speaker has learned the mother's quiet acceptance, and that is exactly the life a bus ticket promises to end. The detail of her "counting under her breath in two languages" (8) works the same way. It is careful and admirable, a woman stretching quarters from a film can, but the counting also measures how tight everything was.

The fourth stanza is where the attitude splits inside a single thought. The mother folds a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it" (14), an image of skill that also hints at something alive being shut in. Then: "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing / was ever let go of, either" (15-16). The first sentence is praise. The line break leaves "Nothing" hanging at the end of line 15, so for a second the reader expects another compliment, and the turn on the next line makes the same thrift sound like a grip. The enjambment actually performs holding on, delaying the release until the word "either." The care that kept nothing from being lost is the same care that would not let the speaker go.

Teague extends this through the packed shirts, ironed "flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed / to a city she has never seen" (19-20). The mother's ironing literally prepares the speaker's departure; her labor is the postage. Yet the metaphor also turns the speaker into a letter, something sent away from the sender, and "never seen" quietly marks how small the mother's own world stayed. Gratitude and distance occupy the same image.

The dryer is the poem's picture of the life being left. The clothes "rise / and fall and rise, a slow tantrum" (21-22), "going nowhere at great speed" (24). A tantrum is a child's frustration, so the speaker seems to see their own restlessness in the drum, and the repetition of "rise" mimics the cycle of shifts and quarters that never adds up to movement. One could read this stanza as contempt for the mother's routine, but the poem doesn't allow pure contempt, because the very next stanza calls her hands builders: "your hands / built me a door" (25-26). Even the door metaphor only partly settles the tension. "Both are thank you. / Only one of them sounds like it" (27-28) admits that leaving is a tribute the mother may hear as rejection, and the speaker has no language to fix that.

The ending keeps this unresolved. The speaker folds "the way she taught me, corners to corners" (30), repeating the mother's gesture even on the last night, so the escape is carried out with her technique. Then the speaker leaves a sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning" (32). It is a small, almost funny gift, but "turning" ties it back to the drum that goes nowhere. Part of the speaker chooses to stay inside the cycle. The poem closes not on the six o'clock bus but in the laundromat, suggesting the speaker can leave Ellery Street without ever being entirely let go of, and that this is both the cost and the thanks.

The night before she leaves home, the speaker of Marisol Teague's "Spin Cycle, Ellery Street" sits in a laundromat doing exactly what her mother did for years, and the poem never gets past that irony. Teague uses the laundromat's circular imagery, the scarred details of the mother's hands, and line breaks that hold on and then let go to show that the speaker can only thank her mother by leaving her. Even the leaving is made out of the mother's habits. So gratitude and escape are not two separate feelings in this poem. They are one act seen from two sides.

The first stanza sets up this inheritance before the speaker admits it. When the change machine "eats my second five," she lets it, "the way she let the landlord / keep the deposit every March." The simile connects her to her mother's patience, but it is patience as giving up, and "every March" turns the loss into a yearly ritual. The memory of quarters fed from a film can, "counting under her breath in two languages," works the same way. The counting is careful and loving, the kind of labor that kept the family going, but it also shows how small and measured that life was, with every quarter tracked.

The third stanza is full of injury. The burn "shaped like a comma on the left thumb" stands out, because a comma is a pause and not a period. The mother's working life is a sentence that never gets to end. The ring "she turned inward so it wouldn't snag" suggests that even her one piece of jewelry, maybe her marriage, was turned to suit the job instead of her. Then the speaker admires her folding a sheet "like a magician closing a box with a dove in it." The image is full of wonder, but the dove is trapped. The line break that follows makes this tension happen on the page: "Nothing was ever lost. Nothing" ends the line, and the reader hangs on that second "Nothing" before the turn to "was ever let go of, either." What started as praise turns into complaint halfway through a sentence. Holding everything together and never letting anything go are the same act, and the enjambment forces us to feel both.

The shirts she ironed "flat as envelopes, sealed, addressed / to a city she has never seen" push this further. The mother's labor literally packages the speaker for departure, sending her child somewhere she herself could not go. The metaphor carries gratitude and guilt together. The dryer, meanwhile, is a "slow tantrum" with clothes "going nowhere at great speed." Calling it a tantrum gives the machine a child's frustration, which sounds like the speaker's own restlessness. The phrase also describes the mother's life, constant motion that stays in place. The repetition "rise / and fall and rise" copies the cycle the speaker is afraid of repeating.

The door metaphor is where the speaker comes closest to stating her attitude. Her repeated "I want to tell her" shows that she doesn't actually say it. Her mother's hands "built me a door," and "I am walking out of it." A reader could argue the mother is mainly confining, since she never let anything go, and the poem partly allows that reading. But a door is something the mother built, so the exit was in some sense her plan. That is why the speaker can say "Both are thank you" and also admit "Only one of them sounds like it." Leaving is the truer thanks, but it is the one her mother might not hear as thanks.

The ending refuses to settle this. The speaker folds "corners to corners," the way she was taught, so the mother's gestures go with her. Then she leaves a sock in the lint trap "so something of mine stays here, turning." This reverses "Nothing was ever lost": she deliberately lets something go, which her mother never did, but she does it so that part of her can stay. The last word, "turning," leaves her both gone and still in the cycle, which is where the poem has kept her all along.

Mr. Ashby, the tutor who narrates Edmund Calloway Wrenne's "The Second Lesson," is telling this story from some time after it happened, and that distance makes his attitude harder to pin down than it first looks. On the surface he admires Clemency and quietly mocks the Pellinghams, a family that cares more about a daughter being "presentable" than about what she can do. But Wrenne's irony doesn't stop at the family. Through dry, deflating descriptions, an image of the cushion that comes back later, and an ending that flips who is teaching whom, the older narrator shows that his younger self's sympathy was mixed up with self-interest. By the last line, what he once called loyalty to the girl has become a confession that he picked up her family's habit of looking away.

Ashby's criticism of the Pellinghams comes mostly through comic details that end up working as accusations. The morning-room is "furnished as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried," and the portraits show Pellinghams "in various attitudes of having been painted." The jokes make the family into possessions and poses, more concerned with how things look than with any life inside them. The schoolroom gets no fire, and the dented globe sits in the corner because "no one had thought the ocean worth repairing." The globe works almost as a symbol of Clemency herself: a whole world of knowledge, damaged and ignored because nobody thinks it matters. Even here, though, Ashby doesn't spare himself. When he agrees that presentability is a worthy goal, he is "conscious of having said something I should be ashamed of before supper." His satire of the household starts with a moment where he goes along with it.

His admiration for Clemency is just as real, but it comes with unease. The simile of the pencil that hovers "as a bird hovers over a field it means to cross" makes her mind deliberate and graceful. The words "means to cross" show that she knows the right answer and chooses not to write it, putting down instead "something a little stupider," a phrase that suggests careful calculation, not confusion. When she says her mother "has had a great deal of practice" judging heads, the line has a double edge. It is a dry joke at Mrs. Pellingham's expense, but it also shows how practiced Clemency is at reading adults. Ashby realizes "I had been weighed, and that the scales were older than I was." The examiner has become the one examined, and his respect for her starts to look like being outmatched.

The paragraph where he decides to keep her secret shows his mixed motives most clearly. Three sentences begin with "I thought," and the list moves from noble reasons to selfish ones. First the two fires, then the married sister, then the image of a house "where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a cushion," a metaphor that makes intelligence into a household nuisance to be blocked out. Then, after "I confess it," come his "forty pounds a year." The order matters, because his sympathy is genuine but it isn't pure, and he wants the reader to feel the drop. The cushion also comes back in a way that complicates things. Clemency hides her real slate "beneath the cushion of the window-seat," the same object the family uses to stop up cleverness. So the secret protects her mind, but it still follows the family's own logic of smothering, and Ashby's two slates turn the house's hiding into a weekly routine that he runs.

The ending makes this a self-judgment. "I flattered myself that I was her ally" admits his vanity, and the empty window-seat replaces "ally" with "accomplice." Someone could read Clemency as manipulative, using a weak tutor for her own ends, but the "older" scales suggest she is protecting herself after years of practice, not scheming. Either way, she has been "teaching me the whole while how to look away." The lesson Ashby actually learns is the one he was hired to give, only backwards. That reversal changes his attitude from fond protectiveness into an uncomfortable, honest guilt.

But Wrenne does not let him keep that role. The passage uses Ashby's irony toward the family, the images he uses for Clemency, and the confessions he makes as an older narrator looking back. Together these show a man whose admiration for the girl and contempt for her family are real but tangled up with cowardice and self-interest. By the end, the missing slate shows that Ashby was never really the teacher, and his sympathy turns into a kind of self-indictment.

Ashby's attitude toward the Pellinghams comes mostly through dry irony. The morning-room is "furnished as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried." That makes the family's comfort sound like a list of property, and the reader starts to suspect that Clemency is treated as one more item on it. Mrs. Pellingham describes her daughter "with the patience of a woman describing a weak chest." The simile turns slowness into an illness the family has bravely put up with. The schoolroom details push this further. Someone decided that "learning wanted no fire," while the morning-room has two fires, and the globe has a dent because no one "thought the ocean worth repairing." The dent is small, but it works as a symbol of the house: knowledge gets damaged and stays damaged because nobody values it. Still, Ashby is not mocking them from a safe distance. He tells Mrs. Pellingham that presentability is "a worthy object" and then immediately admits it was "something I should be ashamed of before supper." His irony is aimed at himself from the first page, which hints that he belongs to the system he criticizes.

Toward Clemency, Ashby's language becomes admiring, almost tender. Her pencil hovers over the right answer "as a bird hovers over a field it means to cross." The simile suggests freedom and intention. The bird "means" to cross, so the wrong answer is a choice, not a failure. But the admiration comes with unease. When he catches her, Ashby feels he has "been weighed," and that "the scales were older than I was." He is the adult, yet the child is doing the judging. Her remark that Mamma "has had a great deal of practice" at judging heads is so dry that it shows she understands her family better than he does. Ashby respects her, but he is also a little afraid of her.

The paragraph where Ashby decides to keep the secret is where his motives split open. He describes a house "where cleverness is a draught to be stopped with a cushion." The metaphor is sympathetic because it shows the family treating intelligence as an annoyance to be blocked out. Then he adds "I confess it" and mentions "my forty pounds a year." The word "confess" is the older narrator judging his younger self and admitting that pity and job security were working together. This is what makes the ending land so hard. The cushion comes back: Clemency keeps her real slate "beneath the cushion of the window-seat," which is the same object the family uses to stop up cleverness. By protecting her, Ashby helped her hide herself the way her family had always hidden her.

The final sentence turns everything around. Ashby "flattered" himself that he was her "ally" but comes to suspect he was only her "accomplice," and that she was "teaching me the whole while how to look away." A reader could see Clemency as manipulative here, using the tutor to cover her escape. I think it is more convincing to read her as self-protective, since she gets nothing from the trick except a hidden place to be right. Either way, the lesson in the title belongs to her. Ashby ends with admiration mixed with shame, because he realizes his kindness was also a way of looking away, which is exactly what the Pellinghams had been doing all along.

In "The Second Lesson," Edmund Calloway Wrenne presents a narrator whose attitude toward Clemency is a mix of admiration and sympathy, but also of guilt about himself. He sees the Pellingham family as cold and foolish, yet he admits that his own reasons for staying quiet are not pure. Through imagery, simile, and a shift in tone at the end, the passage shows a man who thinks he is helping a child but slowly realizes he has been used, and that he has also used her situation to protect himself.

At the start the narrator is critical of the family, and he shows this through description of the house. The morning-room is "warmed by two fires" and furnished "as if the family expected at any hour to be inventoried," which makes the Pellinghams seem concerned with possessions and appearance rather than people. The schoolroom is cold because someone decided "learning wanted no fire," and this shows that the family does not value learning. The dented globe is another example, since "no one had thought the ocean worth repairing." The narrator is mocking them with this detail, and his tone is dry and sarcastic. Mrs. Pellingham's comparison of her daughter's weak mind to "a weak chest" is also made to seem ridiculous.

His attitude toward Clemency is more admiring. When he watches her pencil, he compares it to "a bird hovers over a field it means to cross," which suggests that she is graceful and that her cleverness is natural, and that she is choosing to hold it back. The simile makes her seem delicate but also in control. When she says her mother "has had a great deal of practice" at being right about heads, the narrator notes there is "no insolence in it," so he sees her as wise beyond her years. He says he "had been weighed," which shows he respects her more than he expected to.

However, the narrator is not just sympathetic. When he decides not to tell Mrs. Pellingham, he thinks about a clever girl in a house where cleverness is "a draught to be stopped with a cushion," which is a metaphor that shows what the family would do to her. But he then admits, "I confess it," that he also thought of his "forty pounds a year." This is where his attitude becomes complicated, because his kindness is mixed with fear for his job. The word "confess" shows that he is judging himself, since he is an older narrator looking back.

The ending makes this clearer. He first thought he was her "ally," but when the slate is gone he realizes he was only an "accomplice" and that she had been teaching him "how to look away." This reverses the roles of teacher and pupil. The two slates also show the double life that he helped to create.

In conclusion, the narrator feels sympathy for Clemency and contempt for her family, but he is also ashamed of his own part, and the details and imagery of the passage show all of these feelings together.

In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer apartment looks like the safest place in Norway. It is warm, it is decorated for Christmas, and Torvald has just gotten a promotion that means money will never be tight again. But Ibsen makes the protection and the confinement come from the same source, Torvald's idea that his wife is a fragile thing to be kept and looked after. Because of this, the play suggests that a home built on sheltering someone can never let that person grow up, and Nora's exit at the end is both a liberation and a real loss she has to pay for.

The first act sets up the house as a place of comfort, but the comfort already has rules attached. Torvald greets Nora with animal pet names and teases her about spending money, and he has forbidden her to eat macaroons. She eats them anyway, hiding them and lying about it. This is a small, almost comic detail, but it shows how the home works. Torvald's care is real, he worries about her and gives her money, but it treats her like a child whose appetites need managing. Nora's response is not open rebellion but secrecy, and secrecy turns out to be the only kind of freedom the house allows her.

The bigger secret makes this even clearer. Years earlier, Nora borrowed money from Krogstad to take Torvald to Italy when he was seriously ill, and since a woman could not take out a loan on her own, she forged her father's signature. In a sense Nora is the one who really protected this household. She saved her husband's life and has been secretly copying documents at night to pay off the debt. Ibsen reverses the roles: the "doll" is the actual protector, and the man who thinks he shelters her has been sheltered without knowing it. But she cannot tell him, because his pride and the law both need her to be helpless. The home keeps her safe only as long as she hides what she is capable of.

Ibsen uses the set itself to show the walls closing in. The letterbox, which only Torvald has a key to, holds Krogstad's letter, so the most private object in the house becomes a trap Nora can't open. At the start of the second act the Christmas tree is stripped and its candles are burned down, a picture of the festive home losing its shine. Nora's frantic tarantella, which she dances to keep Torvald away from the mailbox, is a performance of the pretty, lively wife he wants, and it is also an act of desperation. Even her entertainment is a kind of imprisonment.

The climax shows that Torvald's protection was always conditional. When he reads the letter he rages that she has ruined him, and as soon as Krogstad sends back the bond he "forgives" her and offers to shelter her again, like a bird he has rescued. That turn is what convinces Nora. She realizes she went from being her father's doll-child to Torvald's doll-wife, and that the safety she had depended on her never becoming a person.

Still, Ibsen does not make her leaving simple. Nora walks out on her children, and the nurse Anne-Marie, who gave up her own child to raise Nora, reminds the audience what it costs a woman to be without a home. Nora has no money and no clear future. The slam of the door is a triumph, but it is also the sound of someone shutting herself out into the cold. By refusing to make freedom comfortable, Ibsen argues that in a society that only lets women belong as dependents, the home's shelter and its prison cannot be separated, and you can only escape one by giving up the other.

In Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House, the Helmer apartment seems like the safest place a woman in nineteenth-century Norway could hope to live. It is warm and decorated for Christmas, and Torvald's new job at the bank will pay for it. Ibsen builds the play so that every comfort the house gives Nora is also a rule she has to follow, though. The home protects her only while she agrees to be the person it was designed for, and the play suggests that a shelter built on one person's performance is really a stage. That is why Nora's exit at the end is both freedom and a real loss: the walls that kept her in were also the only self she had ever been allowed to have.

The first scene sets up this double meaning with small objects. Nora comes in with packages and a Christmas tree that she tells the maid to hide until it is decorated, and she secretly eats macaroons that Torvald has forbidden. The tree is a lot like Nora. It is something beautiful that gets arranged for display, and Torvald treats her the same way when he calls her by pet names for little birds and squirrels and hands her money as if it were an allowance. Even the macaroons matter. In this house even a cookie has to be hidden, so Nora has to lie to enjoy a harmless pleasure. Still, Ibsen does not pretend the protection is fake. When Mrs. Linde arrives, widowed, worn out, and desperate for work, she shows the audience what waits outside a husband's house for a woman with no money. Next to her, Nora's cage looks like luck, and I think that is the point. The comfort is real, which is exactly what makes it hard to leave.

The secret loan turns the house's logic upside down. Years earlier Nora borrowed money from Krogstad to pay for the trip to Italy that saved Torvald's life, so it turns out the home was being protected by her, not by him. But since a wife could not legally borrow without a man's consent, she forged her father's signature. The same social structure that is supposed to shelter women makes their own acts of protection criminal. Ibsen shows this through the locked letterbox. Krogstad drops his letter exposing the forgery into it, and only Torvald has the key, so a piece of the home meant for privacy becomes the trap closing on Nora. Her wild tarantella, danced to keep Torvald away from the mail, shows how little power she has. Performing is the one tool the house ever taught her to use.

The ending is where the two sides of the home separate. Torvald explodes at Nora, and then, once Krogstad sends back the bond, he forgives her and promises to shelter her like something he has rescued. His forgiveness is what shows Nora she has been a doll first in her father's house and then in her husband's, which makes the title refer to the whole institution rather than one marriage. Ibsen does not make her leaving easy, though. She walks out at night and leaves her children behind, and the nurse, Anne-Marie, who had to give away her own child to survive, reminds us that women in this world pay for every choice. Early audiences thought this was so shocking that Ibsen was pushed into writing a different ending for a German production in which Nora stays for the children. That reaction actually backs up the play's argument, because it shows how strongly people believed a home's protection should outweigh a woman's selfhood. The door slamming at the end is so powerful because it sounds like escape and like loss at once. Nora is free, but she has no shelter yet, and Ibsen leaves us unsure whether the world outside will be any kinder than the dollhouse.

The speaker of "To the Ellery Orchard, at Picking's End" has done everything a father does for a child except own it. Tobias Wrenfield's hired hand speaks to the trees on his last night as if they were family, but every claim of kinship he makes runs into the fact that the law, the bank, and Old Ellery have the stronger claim. Wrenfield uses a contrast between bodily and commercial language, a shift in how the speaker addresses the orchard, and a final curse that is also a plea to be remembered. Together they show that the speaker's pride in his work is exactly what makes losing it hurt. He cannot be proud of the orchard without also being bitter about it.

From the first line the poem sets two ways of knowing the orchard against each other. "You know my hands better than his ledger does" puts the speaker's body next to Ellery's book, and the speaker obviously thinks the hands win. The same split comes back in the sharpest line of the second stanza: "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar." The parallel grammar makes the two men equal for a second, since each one is counting, but what they count is completely different. A bushel is a unit you sell. A scar is something the tree and the man both carry, so the word quietly makes them alike. The Baldwin he "split and bound with twine" was healed the way a broken arm is set. The simile that it "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" gives the tree a person's private resentment, but that resentment is really the speaker's, and he can only express it by lending it to the tree.

The third stanza turns the address sour: "Bear, then. Bear for him." The imperative sounds like permission but reads like an accusation, and the repeated "bear" carries two meanings, bearing fruit and bearing a burden. He complains that the tree "never asked" whose knee was bruised, then admits "A tree is a poor Christian." The line is half a joke, but it shows the speaker knows his grievance has nowhere to go. A tree cannot thank him, and he implies that the man who owns it won't either.

Then comes the turn: "Still, I made you." The word "Still" takes back everything the previous stanza conceded. The repeated negatives, "Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank," list the legal and financial powers that own the orchard only so he can dismiss them. This is where the poem's paradox is clearest. Through his labor the orchard is his, but legally it is not, and he can only assert the first claim by naming the second. The simile "I made you as a man makes a stubborn son" is followed by "by hitting where it hurt and staying near," which may be the most honest moment in the poem. It admits the kinship was built through violence, the same pruning that cut the trees "back to the bone." His love was never gentle, and that makes it more believable.

The fifth stanza's plain, almost flat language shows what being dispossessed looks like. He walks toward Hatch's Mill "with my coat over my arm and nothing in it," paid in silver but still empty-handed. That emptiness sets up the ending. The apple "red as a slapped cheek on a parlor table" carries the violence of the son simile into the lady's parlor, as if the fruit still holds the mark of the hand that raised it. When he asks that one apple "be sour at the core," it is easy to read the line as pure revenge. But the last line, "Let her taste me," changes it. He is not only spoiling her pleasure. He wants to be inside the fruit, noticed by someone who will never know his name. The curse is the only signature a hired man can leave.

Wrenfield's speaker never resolves his feelings, and that is the point. The pride and the grievance come out of the same nine Marches of work, so the closer he gets to claiming the orchard, the more clearly he sees that he has lost it.

He keeps setting the language of the body against the language of money, and he moves the speaker's address from intimacy to bitter command to something close to a curse. He can claim the trees only in the one way the law does not recognize, so his final wish works as revenge and also as a plea to be remembered.

The opening line sets up the conflict as a contest between two kinds of knowledge: "You know my hands better than his ledger does." Hands against ledger is the whole poem in small form. Ellery's relationship to the orchard is written down, while the speaker's is physical and has no record. Line 6 sharpens this with parallel syntax: "He counts you by the bushel, I by the scar." Because the verb is left out the second time, both men seem to be doing the same thing, counting, but in different units. A bushel can be sold. A scar is carried, and it is ambiguous, since it could be the mark on the tree from the pruning hook or the mark on the speaker himself. That ambiguity is the kinship claim, because the wound belongs to both of them. The same thing happens when he says he "cut you back to the bone," giving the tree a skeleton. The Baldwin that "leans now like a man who has been told a joke" gets the speaker's own posture, too. It is a man who takes an insult and "keeps it to himself," and that is exactly what a hired hand has to do.

The third stanza turns that swallowed insult outward. "Bear, then. Bear for him." The clipped imperatives sound like a man giving up, but the pun on "bear" (to produce fruit, and also to endure) lets him accuse the tree of putting up with Ellery as calmly as it put up with him. He then calls a tree "a poor Christian" because it "forgives / nobody, and it thanks nobody." The complaint is unfair, and he seems to know it. A tree can't thank anyone. The grievance really belongs to Ellery, and he aims it at the orchard because the orchard is the only listener he has.

The fourth stanza turns on "Still, I made you," and here pride comes back stronger than before. The repeated "not" in "Not the deed in the courthouse drawer, not the bank" removes every legal claim one by one, as if writing a counter-deed. The stubborn-son simile is the poem's most complicated move. A father who makes a son "by hitting where it hurt and staying near" is harsh but devoted, which describes pruning well. It also points to the paradox at the center of the poem. In ordinary life a son is the father's heir, but here the father is the one who gets disinherited. Even his plea, "Say it, if a tree can say," admits that his claim has no witness who can speak.

The dispossession is made literal in "silver" and a coat with "nothing in it," while the cider press, groaning "like a cow in calf," gets the image of birth that he has lost. Then the ending brings his violence back. The apples are "red as a slapped cheek," which echoes the father's hitting, and he asks that one be "sour at the core." In this passage from Salt Hours, Nell Garrow goes two days without opening a letter that could take her to the city, and Bressan makes it clear that Nell is keeping it shut as much as her father is. Through images of weighting and binding, the repeated rhythm of mending, and a small gesture Nell hides at the end, Bressan shows that Nell resents her father's silent way of deciding her life but loves him too much, and is too shaped by his work, to fight him openly. Because of this, staying and leaving both feel like kinds of being tied down, and the only rebellion she can manage is a private one.

The passage opens with the letter weighted by a stone with a white band, "like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to take off." It's a strange simile for a girl thinking about a clerk's job, but it fits. A forgotten ring is a promise that has outlasted its reason, and it could stand for her parents' marriage after her mother's death or for Nell's own unspoken promise to this beach. Then the narrator says Nell put the stone there herself, and "she told herself that was the only reason." The words "told herself" show she doesn't quite believe her own excuse. The irony is that the thing pinning down her future is something she put there. Later, when she learns her father promised her to Dan Pruett, she thinks "He had built her a Saturday" and set it down "like a stone on a letter." Bressan repeats the image so that Nell's accusation hits her too. She is angry at him for doing exactly what she did, which is why her resentment can never stay pure.

The net is the main image of how the two are tied together. They are "joined by forty feet of brown mesh," which is connection and entanglement at once. When Amos redoes her knot with "a quick small violence of the thumbs," the word "violence" shows the control inside his care: he doesn't ask, he just takes the twine. But the repeated "Over, under, through" gives the work a calming rhythm, and Bressan ties it to Nell's grief. After her mother died, she learned to fill the silence "by working inward from the sound edges," just like mending a hole. So the net isn't only her father's trap. It is the way she survived.

This is why her anger collapses. She tests it "the way you try a plank" and "found it would not hold." Then comes a string of sentences starting with "Because," which pile up reasons the way someone argues with herself, and the last reason is the most exposed: she "had wanted, absurdly, for him to keep holding it." The word "absurdly" is Nell embarrassed by her own tenderness. You could read Amos as a controlling father who gives his daughter no voice, and the Dan Pruett deal backs that up, but Bressan doesn't let that reading stand, because Nell tries it herself and it fails.

The ending complicates things even more. The wind lifts the envelope "like something breathing," as if the letter is alive and waiting. Her father's hands lie still "for the space of three waves," and his silence changes from control to something closer to permission when he says, "You'll want to read that before the light goes." Now it is Nell who answers "Tomorrow," so the delay is clearly hers. Finally she pulls a knot "too tight," then "did not let him see her loosen it." Pulling too hard may be anger, or a too-eager proof that she belongs here. Loosening it fixes the knot by his own lesson about pulled knots, so she obeys him, but in secret. At the same time, loosening is the first small act of letting go. Bressan holds both meanings in one motion, and that is Nell's division exactly: she hasn't decided to stay or leave, only that she will do her untying where he can't see it.

The same images of weight and binding that show Amos holding Nell in place also show Nell holding herself there, so her resentment of him keeps turning into tenderness, and her ambition keeps turning into fear. By the end his silence has shifted from control to something closer to permission, and that is harder for her to bear than control.

The first thing Bressan shows us is the stone on the envelope, and the irony is that "Nell had put the stone there herself." The excuse about the wind is undercut right away by the phrase "she told herself that was the only reason," which tells the reader she does not quite believe it. The stone is also described "like a wedding ring somebody had forgotten to take off." The simile ties the letter to marriage and loyalty, maybe to her dead mother, and it suggests that Nell's bond to home is something she keeps wearing out of habit, not something forced on her. Before the father says a word, she has already weighted down her own future.

The net works the same way. Father and daughter are "joined by forty feet of brown mesh," a literal tie between them that also stands for the family work she would be leaving. When he redoes her knot with "a quick small violence of the thumbs," Bressan puts force and skill in the same phrase. He corrects her, but he is also right. The repeated "Over, under, through" gives the mending a steady, almost hypnotic rhythm, and that rhythm is what keeps her in place. Even her grief takes the shape of the net. After her mother died she learned to fill the quiet "by working inward from the sound edges," so mending has become how she survives, which makes leaving the net feel like leaving the way she copes.

Nell's resentment peaks when she finds out her father promised her to Dan Pruett. "He had built her a Saturday," Bressan writes, and then compares it to setting it on the calendar "like a stone on a letter." This echo is the key to the passage. The father's control is described in exactly the image of Nell's own act, so she can't blame him without blaming herself. She tries anger "the way you try a plank," and it "would not hold." The three sentences beginning with "Because" pile up reasons for not being angry: he was right, the net is familiar, his fingers were warm. The anaphora sounds like Nell arguing with herself, and the last reason, that she had wanted "absurdly, for him to keep holding it," shows that what holds her is love as much as duty.

The ending turns the father's silence around. When the envelope flutters "like something breathing," his needle stops "for the space of three waves," and that pause is the only time his work breaks. Then he says, "You'll want to read that before the light goes." Someone could read this as one more order, but it actually opens the door he had been keeping shut. Nell is the one who puts it off with "Tomorrow." He nods "as though she had told him the weather," holding his feelings back the same way she does. In the final image she pulls a knot "too tight, and did not let him see her loosen it." Over-tightening is her frustration, but quietly loosening it means she fixes it the way he taught her, and she hides that. It is a small gesture that holds the whole conflict: Nell is pulling against him and obeying him in the same motion, and she will not let either of them see which feeling is winning.

At the start of Macbeth, the Macbeths may be the closest couple in all of Shakespeare. He writes to his wife about the witches before he tells anyone else, and she reads his ambition better than he does. The murder of Duncan should seal that closeness, since now two people share something no one else in Scotland knows. Instead Shakespeare shows the secret slowly turning their marriage from a partnership into two separate cells. Because keeping a murder hidden depends on controlling what you say, even to the person who helped you, the bond that the secret creates is also what wears it away. The play suggests that loyalty built on concealment cannot last, because it needs the same silence that destroys it.

The binding effect is clearest on the night of the murder. Macbeth comes back carrying the bloody daggers, too shaken to return them, and Lady Macbeth takes them back herself and smears the sleeping grooms with blood. In this scene their roles fit together. Her nerve covers for his panic, and his act makes her plan real. Shakespeare even shows them finishing each other's thoughts in short, broken exchanges, so the rhythm of the dialogue makes them sound like one mind split between two voices. Blood is the symbol that joins them, because they both have it on their hands. Then the knocking at the gate interrupts them, a reminder that the outside world is right there. The secret only exists because there is a "them" and an "everyone else," so from the first scene their closeness and their isolation from Scotland are the same thing.

The isolation starts to turn inward once Macbeth becomes king. He arranges Banquo's murder without telling his wife and keeps her in the dark on purpose, which reverses the letter from Act 1. He might think he is protecting her, but the effect is that the secret now has layers, and she is outside one of them. At the banquet, when Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost, Lady Macbeth covers for him again, explaining his fits to the lords and then sending the guests away. On the surface this looks like the daggers scene repeated, but it is hollow. She is defending a crime she wasn't told about, and the guests leave suspicious. Her loyalty is now just damage control, and the dramatic irony (we know what Macbeth sees and she does not) shows how far apart they have grown while still standing next to each other.

By Act 5 the secret has fully separated them. Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, trying to wash blood off her hands that is no longer there, while a doctor and a gentlewoman listen. Someone could read this as the secret finally coming out, almost a confession that might bring relief. That reading doesn't hold up, though, because she says it alone, asleep, to people she can't see, and it frees nothing. It is the opposite of the night of the murder: then they shared one secret between two people, and now each carries a private version of it. When Macbeth hears she has died, he responds with numb exhaustion instead of grief, saying life means nothing. The man who once wrote to her first now hardly reacts to her death.

Shakespeare's tragedy shows that a secret can make a couple feel closer than anyone else, but only by cutting them off from everyone around them, and in the end from each other. In a play where killing a king upsets the whole natural order, it makes sense that the Macbeths' private loyalty grows into a kind of disorder too. The partnership was real, but because it depended on silence, it was ruining itself from the beginning.

At the start of Macbeth, the Macbeths may be the closest couple in all of Shakespeare. They finish each other's plans, they call each other by tender names, and they agree to a murder almost the way other couples agree to a wedding date. But the secret of Duncan's murder, which seems at first to make them partners in everything, ends up working like a wall built down the middle of their marriage. Shakespeare suggests that guilt can be shared out at the beginning but cannot be held together, because keeping it hidden means each person ends up guarding it alone. The play's real tragedy is not only that a king dies but that the crime meant to bind husband and wife ends up leaving each of them completely alone.

The secret starts out as something they own together. When Macbeth sends his wife the letter about the witches' prophecy, he is already pulling her into a circle no one else is in, except Banquo, who also heard the witches and therefore becomes a danger. Lady Macbeth answers by taking on the plan as hers too, and on the night of the murder the work is split between them like chores. He kills Duncan. She takes the daggers back and smears the sleeping grooms with blood when he is too shaken to return to the room. Even the blood imagery shows them as a pair. Both of them have red hands, and she tells him a little water will clean them. In this scene the secret really is a refuge: Macbeth is falling apart, and his wife's calm is the only thing holding him up. Their closeness depends on nobody else knowing.

Yet the same scene already shows the cracks. Macbeth hears a voice saying he has murdered sleep, and his wife cannot hear it and brushes it off. They are standing in the same dark hallway, but they are not having the same experience. Sleep matters here because it is the one place a person cannot keep watch over what they might say, and from now on neither of them can rest. Then the secret splits. Macbeth arranges Banquo's murder without telling his wife and tells her to stay innocent of the knowledge until it is done. It is easy to read this as him protecting her, but it also means the partnership is finished. He has learned that a secret is safest with one keeper, so he starts keeping secrets from the only person who shared the first one.

The banquet scene shows how isolating the secret has become. Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost in his chair, and Lady Macbeth covers for him in front of the lords, saying her husband has had fits since he was young. She is still loyal, but her loyalty only works as performance in front of other people, and she cannot see what he sees. The secret that once let them talk freely now forces them to watch each other in public. Outside their circle, Scotland itself is closed off: Macduff runs away, Malcolm is suspicious, and the country is full of people who know something is wrong and cannot say so.

Some readers see Lady Macbeth as the stronger villain, the one who pushed her husband into it. The ending makes that harder to believe. She is the one who breaks, sleepwalking and scrubbing at blood only she can see, confessing details in front of a doctor and a gentlewoman. Her hands, which she once thought water could clean, are now the proof that the secret is still inside her. In a way the sleepwalking is the only honest moment she has left, and she has it alone, with Macbeth nowhere around. When he hears she has died, he hardly reacts and moves on to his speech about life meaning nothing. A partnership that once could not be separated ends with two people who each fell apart without the other knowing. For Shakespeare, loyalty built on hiding something is not loyalty that lasts. The secret becomes their whole world, and in the end it leaves each of them alone in it.
